# Crank, connecting rod and flywheel (`crank_connecting_rod`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A crank is an arm on a shaft with a pin set off-centre. A connecting rod, hinged at both ends, joins the pin to something that moves to and fro, so rotation becomes reciprocation (a water wheel working a saw or pump) or the reverse (a treadle or piston turning a wheel). The stroke is twice the crank radius. Twice per turn the rod lines up with the crank and cannot turn it (dead centres); a heavy flywheel carries the shaft through these points and evens out the motion. A straight-moving end needs a guide (crosshead) or the rod bends it sideways.
- Pitfalls:
  - No flywheel, so the machine sticks at dead centre or runs in jerks
  - A rigid rod without a joint at the sliding end
  - Assuming the crank is obvious and ancient everywhere; the crank with connecting rod was rare before the 15th c.
- History: china: c. 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD – hand crank on rotary winnowing fans (Han tomb models); 1313 Wang Zhen shows a water wheel driving furnace bellows through crank, connecting rod and piston rod; rome: 3rd c. AD – relief of a water-powered stone saw with crank and connecting rod at Hierapolis; sawmills of the 6th c. at Gerasa and Ephesus; islamic: 9th c. – Banu Musa use a crank-like element in automata; 1206 al-Jazari's twin-cylinder pump driven by crank and connecting rod; europe: c. 830 – crank-turned grindstone in the Utrecht Psalter; c. 1420–1430 carpenter's brace and the compound crank with connecting rod (anonymous engineer of the Hussite Wars); flywheels on cranks by the 15th c.
- Read:
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
  - T. Ritti, K. Grewe & P. Kessener, A relief of a water-powered stone saw mill on a sarcophagus at Hierapolis and its implications, Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
